examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Normal Random Variable on an Unbounded Interval Using the Complement
examples.worked_solution:
Given a normal random variable $Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),$ we have

$$
P(Y \geq y) = P \left( Z \geq \dfrac{y-\mu}{\sigma} \right)
$$

where $Z \sim N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu = 5$ and $\sigma = 4.$

First, we transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 2.92) & =P(Z\ge \frac{2.92-5}{4}) \\  & =P(Z\ge -0.52)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070250/assets/049e4733082674668ebbe2c5a710cd847f1db16d26fdcd2af6e603941efdffe7.png)

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $\Phi(z)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge -0.52) & =1-P(Z<-0.52) \\  & =1-P(Z\le -0.52) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.52)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
\Phi(-0.52) =0.3015.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge -0.52) & =1-Φ(-0.52) \\  & =1-0.3015 \\  & =0.6985.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
P(Y \geq 2.92) = 0.6985.
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Given a normal random variable $X∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$
P(X<x)=P(Z<\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =3$ and $\sigma =6.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<13.5) & =P(Z<\frac{13.5-3}{6}) \\  & =P(Z<1.75) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.75) \\  & =Φ(1.75)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070250/assets/e024a5ac6bdd86c88c6ed6cbe3a647281c63e6934c3830288fa01c1d51997e4a.png)

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(1.75)=0.9599.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(X<13.5)=0.9599.
$$
